sections.h2: Who values and who bills a Pulaski County property?
sections.html:
Two Somerset offices split the job. The Property Valuation Administrator places a value on each parcel and answers at (606) 679-1812. The Pulaski County Sheriff's tax office prints the bill and collects it, with staff on duty weekdays from 8:00 AM until 4:00 PM and a tax mailbox at taxes@pulaskisheriff.com.

Neither office votes on rates. Each taxing district sets its own levy, from the fiscal court to the school board. Three public school systems serve the county, namely Pulaski County, Somerset Independent and Science Hill Independent, so the school share of a bill follows the district lines.

The sheriff handles more than houses. Its FAQ lists real estate with school taxes, tangible property, franchise and gas taxes, undeveloped land, oil, and limestone, sand and gravel.

sections.h2: What does the Pulaski County sheriff's calendar look like?
sections.html:
The sheriff's own FAQ says bills begin to be mailed during early October. The steps below follow that page, and the 5 percent January step agrees with KRS 134.015.

Pulaski County sheriff: amount owed by payment date
When paidAmount
October 1 to November 1Bill less a 2 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Base amount
January 1 to January 31Base amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Base amount plus 21 percent
April 16 onwardPay the County Clerk, (606) 679-2042

Counter payments can be cash, check or card, and card users pay a small added fee. The office refuses part payments and wants the full bill at once. A mailed check comes back with a receipt if you enclose a stamped return envelope. A lost bill is replaced at no charge.

sections.h2: What would a median Pulaski County home owe the state?
sections.html:
Kentucky's rate for 2025 is 10.6 cents on every hundred dollars of assessment. With Census QuickFacts listing a median value of $166,900 for Pulaski County homes, the state portion works out to about $176.91. Local districts stack their rates above that figure.

The older or disabled owner deduction changes the base. At $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, it leaves $117,800 taxable on that median house and brings the state portion to about $124.87. The sheriff's FAQ still quotes an older deduction amount, so use the Department of Revenue figure and confirm it with the PVA when applying.

Paying inside the October 1 to November 1 window earns the 2 percent discount on the whole bill.

sections.h2: How do I dispute a Pulaski County valuation?
sections.html:
Every Kentucky appeal opens with a meeting at the PVA office, whether the parcel is a Lake Cumberland cottage or a farm near Eubank. The roll can be inspected for thirteen days from May's first Monday. At the meeting the PVA must explain how the number came about and record your claimed value, anything agreed and the result.

  • The appeal reaches the clerk on the first workday after the roll closes.
  • A local board of property owners hears cases about a month later, in a session of up to five days.
  • Supporting papers are required: land and building descriptions, insurance policies, construction cost and sales listings. A file without them is rejected.
  • Anyone you hire to speak for you must come from the statutory list and hold your signed authorization.

If bills print before the board rules and the final value exceeds your claim, a supplemental bill follows for the gap.

sections.h2: Who owes the tax when a Pulaski County house sells mid year?
sections.html:
The sheriff's FAQ is direct: whoever held the parcel at the start of the year owes the fall bill, though a closing may prorate it. Your closing attorney can explain how the contract divides the year, and the tax office can tell you whether the parcel shows paid or open.

State law agrees. Under KRS 134.015 the tax is the owner's personal debt as of the assessment date, and a lien described in KRS 134.420 stays on the land for eleven years. Lenders that escrow often pay the bills they hold. The sheriff still stresses that the bill is the homeowner's duty, so give your lender a copy if your mailing address changed.

A seller moving away should also tell the PVA, because the older owner deduction follows the person and the buyer must apply separately.

sections.h2: What follows after April 15 in Pulaski County?
sections.html:
On April 16 the sheriff passes unpaid bills to the County Clerk. Each turns into a certificate of delinquency backed by a lien. A buyer of a delinquent bill collects the tax plus 12 percent a year and costs such as attorney and filing fees, according to the sheriff's FAQ. The house itself is not auctioned at that stage.

The clerk adds interest of 1 percent monthly. A Department of Revenue example shows a $1,000 bill reaching $1,254 on transfer and about $1,387.79 within five business days, with the county attorney's commission and postage added after notices go out. Notices go out before a sale, which the law places between 90 and 135 days after transfer.

Paying the clerk before the sale day keeps an investor from acquiring the bill.

sections.h2: What stands out about Pulaski County for someone selling?
sections.html:
Pulaski County dates to December 1798, when land from Lincoln and Green counties was combined and named after Count Casimir Pulaski. Somerset is the seat, joined by Burnside, Eubank, Ferguson and Science Hill. The county covers about 658 square miles of land, third largest in Kentucky, with Lake Cumberland and its houseboat trade in the south. The county's own figures list an average elevation of 974 feet, 58.9 degrees as the yearly mean temperature, 47.29 inches of rain and 12.6 inches of snow. Alcohol sales are limited to Somerset and Burnside.

Roads are a strength. US 27 runs north and south, Kentucky 80 east and west, the Cumberland Expressway reaches US 27 north of Somerset, and Kentucky 914 loops the city. Interstate 75 lies about 28 miles east, and Lexington is 76 miles north. Somerset Community College keeps a campus on Monticello Street, and Lake Cumberland Regional Airport serves general aviation at the south end of town.

  • July 2025 population estimate: 67,384, a 3.6 percent rise over 2020.
  • Housing: 26,210 households, 72.5 percent of homes lived in by owners.
  • Typical home value $166,900; typical gross rent $803.
  • Midpoint household income of $51,898, with 20.1 percent below the poverty line.
  • 129 building permits in 2025.

Visitors come for Lake Cumberland, the Mill Springs Battlefield, Somersplash Water Park, the Master Musicians Festival in July and the Somernites Cruise on the fourth Saturday of each month from April to October. Rail service on the Norfolk Southern line and the airport round out the access, and Somerset sits 129 miles northwest of Knoxville and 128 miles southeast of Louisville. A house with roof, septic or shoreline trouble can still go to a direct cash buyer, with any tax owed settled at closing.

faqs.q: Can I pay a Pulaski County tax bill by card?
faqs.a: Yes, at the counter of the sheriff's tax office, with a small fee added for cards. Cash, checks and mailed checks also work, but the full bill must be paid at once because part payments are refused.

faqs.q: What are the extra charges after January in Pulaski County?
faqs.a: The sheriff lists 5 percent for January and 21 percent for February 1 through April 15. After that the County Clerk takes payment.

faqs.q: When does the Pulaski County early discount apply?
faqs.a: From October 1 through November 1, a 2 percent discount comes off the bill. The base amount is due November 2 through December 31.

faqs.q: Where do I claim the older owner deduction in Pulaski County?
faqs.a: Call the PVA at (606) 679-1812. The state set it at $49,100 for owners 65 and up or totally disabled, for 2025 and 2026.

faqs.q: Will the sheriff auction my house over unpaid Pulaski County tax?
faqs.a: Not at the sheriff stage. After April 15 the bill goes to the County Clerk and can be sold to an investor, who then holds a lien with 12 percent yearly interest and costs.
